processing: Light oxidation and ball-rolling in the Anxi style, finished green or with a light roast; the same cultivar is also made into green and black tea elsewhere in Fujian.
harvest_season: Spring (late April to early May) and autumn (October); it sprouts early and yields heavily, so summer lots are common and cheap.
appearance_dry: Tight, slightly fuzzy green pellets with pale downy tips showing here and there.
appearance_wet: Elliptical leaves with sharply serrated edges and fine white down on the underside of the young leaves.
taste_profile: Jasmine-like florals and a brisk, slightly sharp sweetness, a lighter body than Tieguanyin and a clean, quick finish.

brewing.notes: Rinse once, short steeps, water just off the boil, porcelain gaiwan. It brews up quickly and can turn sharp if steeped long, so pour fast.

vintage_note: Sold by season like Tieguanyin, spring and autumn of the current year, and meant to be drunk within the year, kept sealed and cold. It is one of the cheapest Anxi oolongs and is often sold unnamed as part of a Tieguanyin or se zhong blend.
description:
Mao Xie, hairy crab, is the Anxi cultivar with the odd name and the jasmine nose: a fast-growing, heavy-yielding bush that makes a bright, floral, inexpensive ball-rolled oolong and quietly fills a lot of cheap Tieguanyin tins.

The name describes the plant. The young leaves carry fine white hairs on their undersides and the leaf edges are sharply serrated, which someone decided looked like a crab's hairy claws. By the traditional account the cultivar was found in Fumei village, Daping township, in Anxi county in the early twentieth century, and it is counted among the four main Anxi cultivars with Tieguanyin, Ben Shan and Huang Dan. It sprouts early, tolerates poor soil and crops heavily, which is why it spread.

It is processed like Tieguanyin, lightly oxidised and ball-rolled, usually in the green style, sometimes with a light roast, and because the leaf is thinner it needs a gentler hand in the shaking stage. The dry pellets are a little fuzzy from the down; the cup is pale gold, with a jasmine-like aroma, a brisk sweetness, and a light body that finishes quickly.

Brew it short and hot in a gaiwan and drink the first four or five steeps; it is not a tea with hidden depths, and long steeps only bring out a sharp edge. It is a pleasant morning oolong and a sensible choice when you want Anxi flowers without Anxi prices.

It is sold by season, spring and autumn, and should be drunk fresh, within the year. Under its own name it is cheap and honest; unnamed, it is a frequent component of low-priced Tieguanyin and of se zhong blends. If you like its brightness, Huang Jin Gui is the other light, fragrant Anxi cultivar worth comparing it with.
sources_note: The Fumei / Daping origin and the early-twentieth-century date (around 1907 is usually cited) follow the traditional Anxi account.
